subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Child Labor in Coffee
description: One-minute skill: Child Labor in Coffee.

hook.text: The US Department of Labor lists coffee as a product commonly produced using child labor in multiple countries.

buildup.text: When prices crash, families who can't afford hired workers send children to pick cherries instead of going to school.

discovery.text: An estimated 1.5 million children work in coffee farming—many in hazardous conditions with chemicals and sharp tools.

twist.text: The root cause isn't cultural acceptance—it's poverty. When families earn enough, children go to school instead.

climax.text: The most effective lever against child labor in coffee is simply paying farmers a living wage.

punchline.text: Low prices don't just hurt farmers. They steal childhoods.

quiz.question: What is the root cause of child labor in coffee farming?
options: Poverty—when families can't afford workers, children pick instead

details.summary: Child labor remains a significant problem in coffee production, particularly in Africa and Central America. Children help with harvesting, sorting, and sometimes spraying chemicals. Poverty drives families to rely on every member's labor.
details.whyItMatters: Child labor in coffee is a human rights issue that consumers rarely see. Addressing it requires increasing farmer incomes, not just policing supply chains.
takeaways: Child labor persists in many coffee-producing regions
Economic poverty is the primary driver of the problem
Higher farm-gate prices are essential to systemic solutions

faq.question: How widespread is child labor in coffee production?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest millions of children work in coffee worldwide. A 2016 study found child labor on coffee farms in at least 17 countries. The extent varies: some children help families during harvest while others miss school entirely. Data is limited in the most affected regions.

faq.question: What can consumers do about child labor in coffee?
faq.answer: Buy certified or direct-trade coffee from companies with transparent supply chains. Support organizations working with farming communities on education and economic development. Recognize that the root cause is poverty and that paying more for coffee is part of the solution.
